Confirmed — this is not a real bug. With genuine touch-device emulation (verified `hover:hover` and `pointer:fine` both `false`), all 8 cards correctly show the default state — no chips, no hover-swap image, nothing stuck open.

This isn't a real bug in the component — it's a testing-method artifact. I tested with genuine touch-device emulation (Playwright's `hasTouch: true, isMobile: true`, and directly confirmed `window.matchMedia('(hover: hover)')` and `(pointer: fine)` both evaluate to `false` in that context — a true no-hover-capability device). Under that, all 8 cards render correctly: "Front" image, price visible, no chips, nothing stuck open.

`HOVER_CAPABLE_QUERY` is `@media (hover: hover) and (pointer: fine)` — deliberately checking *input capability*, not viewport width. That's correct: a real phone has no mouse, so this query genuinely never matches there, regardless of screen size.

What's almost certainly happening in your screenshot: if you're testing "mobile" by narrowing your actual desktop browser window (rather than using a real device or DevTools' device-toolbar touch emulation), the browser still has a real mouse/trackpad — `hover:hover`/`pointer:fine` stay `true` no matter how narrow the window gets. So if your cursor was sitting over Card 1's area when you looked, it genuinely, correctly triggered the hover reveal — a real mobile phone user could never reproduce this, since they have no cursor to hover with in the first place.

So: nothing to fix here. If you want to test true mobile behavior going forward, Chrome DevTools' device toolbar (with touch simulation on) or a real device will correctly show `hover: none`, unlike just shrinking the window.

Think of Einstein as a separate notebook-keeper watching your shop, not something your own website writes in itself.

**Two separate conversations happen with Einstein, at two different times — writing and reading:**

1. **Writing (when a shopper views a product):** Your app taps Einstein on the shoulder and says "hey, this visitor just looked at product X." That's `einstein.sendViewProduct(product)` — a method that already exists in this codebase's `useEinstein()` hook. Einstein writes it down in **its own notebook**, not in anything Zimmermann's servers or your browser store.

2. **Reading (when you want to show "Recently Viewed"):** Later, your app asks Einstein "what has this visitor looked at recently?" — `einstein.getRecommendations('viewed-recently-einstein', [])`. Einstein flips through its notebook and hands back a short list: product IDs, plus a name/image/url from **Einstein's own copy** of your catalog (fed to it periodically, not live).

**What ties the "writing" and "reading" together — a cookieId.** Every time your app talks to Einstein, it includes a token identifying the visitor (like a library card number). Write with that card, read with that card, get back what that same card looked at. If the shopper is logged in, you can *also* hand over a `userId` — Einstein can link that across different devices, so "recently viewed" would genuinely follow you from phone to laptop. That's the one thing browser storage structurally can't do.

**Why we don't just trust the name/image Einstein hands back:** it's from Einstein's own periodically-refreshed copy of the catalog, not live Zimmermann data — a price change or a sold-out size wouldn't show up immediately. So the real pattern is: take *only the IDs* Einstein returns, then call our own `getProducts` (real SFCC/SCAPI) to fetch current, live product data for exactly those IDs.

**The interesting part for you:** our existing architecture is already shaped for this. `recentlyViewedProductFetch.ts` takes a list of product IDs and fetches live data for them — it has no idea whether those IDs came from `localStorage` or from Einstein. Swapping the *source* of the ID list (from `useRecentlyViewedHistory`'s browser storage to `einstein.getRecommendations`) would be a fairly contained change, not a rearchitecture — assuming DNT is resolved and Einstein is actually deployed on a real Zimmermann site, both separate, already-known blockers.

detail: now walk me through how our local tracking approach works for now, ELI5 - the goal behind this is too gauge how big of a change is required to move from local tracking to EINSTEIN once it's available
local tracking walkthrough: one hook swap to migrate to Einstein
text:
Same two moments — writing and reading — except both happen entirely inside the shopper's own browser, with no outside service involved at all.

**Writing (when a shopper views a product):** PDP calls `markProductViewed(product.id)` — from `useRecentlyViewedHistory.ts`. Instead of mailing that to Einstein's notebook, we write it straight into the **shopper's own browser's notebook** (`localStorage`) — sitting on their machine, not on any server. That notebook holds at most 24 product IDs, most-recent first, no duplicates.

**Reading (when we want to show "Recently Viewed"):** We don't ask anyone — we just open that same browser's notebook and read the ID list straight out, instantly, no network call involved for this part. Then — and this is the part that matters for your question — we do **exactly the same thing** the Einstein version would do: hand that ID list to `recentlyViewedProductFetch.ts`, which calls the real `getProducts` SCAPI endpoint to fetch live product data (price, image, name) for those specific IDs. That function has no idea whether the IDs came from a browser notebook or from Einstein — it just wants a list of IDs.

**The one real structural difference:** there's no "library card" (cookieId) tying anything together — it's just "whatever's written in *this one browser's* notebook." Switch to your phone, and that phone has its own empty notebook; nothing carries over. That's the cross-device gap we already know about and can't fix with this approach.

**So, gauging the migration — here's the actual split:**

- **Already Einstein-shaped, untouched by a migration:** `recentlyViewedProductFetch.ts` (fetch real data for a list of IDs), `recentlyViewedCard.ts` / `recentlyViewedFullHistoryCard.ts` (map product → card), the rail, the grid, the Full History page. None of this cares where the ID list came from.
- **The one piece that's local-storage-specific:** `useRecentlyViewedHistory.ts`. It's the only thing that owns *both* "write to browser storage" and "read from browser storage."
- **The migration, concretely:** swap that one hook. `markProductViewed` becomes a call to `einstein.sendViewProduct` at the same PDP call site it's already wired to. Reading `recentlyViewedIds` becomes calling `einstein.getRecommendations(...)` and pulling the ID list out of `.recs[].id`. Everything downstream — fetch, map, render — doesn't change at all.

Bottom line: this is a small, contained swap, not a rearchitecture — one hook replaced, one call site updated, assuming DNT and platform deployment are sorted out separately.

**Confirmed, precisely.** Product `4673TS251`'s catalog data has a broken image reference. Checked directly, not guessed:

- The `medium` viewType group (what our rail mapper reads) has 9 images. The **first one** — exactly the one our code picks — returns **HTTP 404**:
  `.../Sites-zimmermann-catalog/en_AU/v1788853141561/images/1.4673ts251...jpg`
- Every other image in that same group (index 1 onward) uses a completely different, normal URL pattern (`.../default/dw<hash>/images/...`) and returns **HTTP 200** fine — I checked one directly.

So this is a genuine **catalog/BM data problem for this one product** — a stale or never-published locale-specific image reference sitting in slot 0 of an otherwise-healthy image group. It's not something wrong with how our mapper reads the data; it's correctly reading exactly what the catalog gives it, and what the catalog gives it for this one slot is broken.

**But it does expose a real gap in our code:** `selectPrimaryImage` (`recentlyViewedCard.ts`) blindly trusts `images[0]` with no fallback — so when that first image happens to be broken, the card still gets built (the string itself is non-empty, so our `null`-check doesn't catch it), it just renders with a dead image URL. This is exactly the `ZimmProductCardMedia` `onError`-fallback idea that came up earlier in this session and was left open — now we have a real, reproducible case pointing at it.

Two separate things to decide:
1. **Flag the catalog data** — a stale image reference on this specific product, for whoever owns BM/catalog data to fix at the source.
2. **Code-level resilience** — add an `onError` fallback so a single broken image doesn't sink the whole card (try the next image in the group, or degrade gracefully). This touches `ZimmProductCardMedia`, a shared component used everywhere (PDP, PLP, Wishlist, Home, not just Recently Viewed) — same "shared component, confirm scope" situation as the hover-grow question earlier.

detail: how will the fallback work/behave?
how will the fallback work/behave? ELI5
fallback mechanism: onError listener swaps to next image candidate
text: Like trying a locked door, then just moving on to the next one — the shopper never sees you jiggling the handle, only whichever door actually opened. **The mechanism:** an `` tag can tell us when it fails to actually load (a real browser event called `onError` — it fires the moment the browser tries the URL and gets back a 404 or similar). Right now our code never listens for that; it picks one image URL and if it's dead, that's just... a dead image. The fallback means: listen for that failure, and when it happens, swap in the *next* candidate image instead. **Concretely, for this exact product:** the "medium" image group has 9 photos. Today we always show photo #1 (broken). With the fallback: 1. Browser tries to load photo #1. 2. It fails (404). 3. Our code notices and swaps the ``'s `src` to photo #2 instead. 4. Photo #2 loads fine (we already confirmed this one works) — shopper sees a real image. **What the shopper actually experiences:** in the success case (like this one), basically nothing — a 404 comes back near-instantly, so the swap to photo #2 happens within a fraction of a second, before most people would even notice a flicker. It's not a visible "retry" spinner or anything — just the correct image shows up, maybe a beat later than if it had been right the first time. **Bounded, not endless:** we'd try a small number of candidates (however many real images that group has, or a capped number) — not loop forever hammering broken URLs. **The one case worth deciding now: what if *every* candidate fails?** (a worse catalog problem than what we're looking at, but possible). Two honest options: show a neutral placeholder box, or don't render the card at all — matching how this codebase already treats "no usable image whatsoever" today (it drops the card rather than show something broken). **Where this lives:** `ZimmProductCardMedia` — the one shared component that actually renders the `` — not the Recently Viewed mapper. The mapper's job would just change slightly: hand over a short ordered list of candidate images instead of committing to one upfront.

Confirmed — click mechanically succeeds once properly hovered, but `aria-checked` never flips. This is purely the missing-handler wiring, not a stacking/overlay bug. Let me verify Add to Bag the same correct way, and confirm no network call fires.

**Root cause found — a genuine, pre-existing wiring gap, not something broken by anything in this session's work.**

`overrides/app/pages/recentlyViewed/index.tsx` builds every card straight from the mapper's output with nothing added on top:

```tsx
const cards = products.map((product) => selectRecentlyViewedFullHistoryCard(product, formatPrice))...
```

`selectRecentlyViewedFullHistoryCard` is a pure, stateless data mapper (by its own design — no React, no hooks) — it has never returned `onSizeChipSelect`, `selectedSizeChipValue`, or `onAddToBag`, and the page container never adds them either. Since all three are *optional* on `ZimmProductCardPlpVariation`, this compiles clean with no type error — nothing catches it.

`ZimmProductCard` always renders the size-chip picker and the Add to Bag button for the `plp` variation regardless of whether handlers are supplied (`showSizeChips`/`showBag` are keyed off variation, not handler presence). So both controls are fully visible and genuinely clickable — the click itself lands correctly — but every click silently no-ops, because there's nothing listening. That's why it "doesn't seem to work": no error, no visual feedback, no network call, just quiet.

**Verified precisely, live, not assumed:**
- Clicked a size chip on the real Full History page → click succeeds mechanically, `aria-checked` never flips.
- Clicked Add to Bag → click succeeds mechanically, zero `POST /basket` requests fire, zero console/page errors.

**One dead end worth mentioning, so you know it was checked and ruled out:** I initially suspected a stacking-context bug (the stretched product-name-link overlay intercepting the click, similar to a known carousel fix elsewhere in this same recipe). Disproved it myself — once a card is genuinely hovered first (as a real shopper would), the click reaches the real chip/button cleanly every time. My first test's failure was my own script clicking a chip that hadn't been hovered yet, not a real product bug. This is isolated to the missing handlers, not a shared-component defect.

**What a real fix would need:** the container has no per-card "currently selected size" state today, and no basket-mutation call at all (unlike PLP's own page, which already calls the real add-to-bag mutation). Fixing this means adding real state management for selection and wiring a real `onAddToBag` handler — the same shape as the `LiveSizeSelectionGrid` wrapper I built for the Storybook story, but with actual page-level state and a real basket call instead of local-only state.

Want me to implement that now?

Let me confirm one more detail — whether PLP's own mapper includes these handlers (to see if the "mapper doesn't own handlers" pattern is consistent across both).

**PLP's pattern, concretely** (`overrides/app/pages/product-list/index.tsx`):

- **Selection state**: a small wrapper component, `ProductListCard` (line 150), sits between the page and `ZimmProductCard`. It owns its own `useState<string | undefined>` for `selectedSizeChipValue` and a `handleSizeChipSelect` that updates that state. Because React creates one `ProductListCard` instance per rendered card, each card automatically gets its own independent state for free — no page-level map needed. Its own comment confirms this is deliberately the same pattern as `zimmProductCard/index.stories.tsx`'s `LiveSizeSelectionCard`.
- **Add to Bag**: built inline per search hit inside the render loop (line 669) — resolves the correct orderable ID (`representedProduct?.id ?? productId`, handling the master-vs-variant SKU distinction), calls the real `addItemToNewOrExistingBasket` mutation (from `useShopperBasketsMutationHelper()`), then a success/error toast.
- **The mapper itself** (`productListCardMapper.ts`) — confirmed it returns none of these three fields either. Same split as Recently Viewed's own mapper: the mapper stays pure data, the page container wires the interactive parts. That part of the architecture is already consistent between the two surfaces.

**One real gap in PLP's own version, worth knowing before copying it:** `selectedSizeChipValue` is cosmetic only. Clicking a chip highlights it, but `handleAddToBag` always adds the search hit's own already-resolved `representedProduct`/`productId` at quantity 1 — it never looks at which chip is selected. PLP's own file calls itself a "quick test integration... not the final PLP implementation," and this is exactly why: a search hit represents one specific variant already, so "select a different size" has no obvious different product ID to switch to without a master→variants lookup PLP doesn't do today.

**Recently Viewed is actually better positioned to do this correctly, not just copy the shortcut:** `recentlyViewedProductFetch.ts` already requests `expand: [...,'variations']` — the full product record, every variant, not just one resolved hit. That means a real fix here *could* make the selected chip actually resolve to that variant's real orderable ID before adding to bag, instead of always adding whatever the default variant happens to be.

So there's a real fork to decide before I build anything:
1. **Mirror PLP exactly** — cosmetic size selection, always adds the default variant regardless of chip. Fastest, consistent with the existing precedent, but knowingly replicates PLP's own acknowledged shortcut.
2. **Build it correctly for Recently Viewed** — selecting a size actually changes what gets added to bag, using the variation data that's already being fetched. More correct, but more work, and diverges from how PLP currently behaves.

Which do you want?

text:
Let me systematically check every real consumer of `ZimmProductCard` and every interactive prop it exposes — not just size chips.

Only 3 real consumers exist — the Rail (which never renders content/chips at all for its variation), PLP, and the Recently-Viewed Grid. So the actual interactive surface to check is narrow: `onSizeChipSelect` (already checked), `onAddToBag` (already checked), and `onNotifyMe` — on both PLP and the Grid.

`onNotifyMe` reveals something different and important — let me confirm the exact gating logic for all three interactive props side by side.

Confirmed the exact difference: `showBag`/`showSizeChips` are read straight from the static `VARIATION_CONFIG` table with no check on whether a handler exists. `showNotifyMe` is the only one of the three actually *computed* with a co-requirement (`Boolean(isUnavailable) && Boolean(onNotifyMe)`) — that's why it's the one exception.

**Full map — every real consumer × every interactive prop** (only 3 real consumers exist: PLP, the Recently-Viewed Grid, and the Rail; the Rail uses `variation: 'recentlyViewed'`, which never mounts `ZimmProductCardContent` at all, so none of this applies there):

| Prop | PLP | Recently-Viewed Grid |
|---|---|---|
| **Size chips** (`onSizeChipSelect`) | Renders, click highlights the chip — but cosmetic: `handleAddToBag` never looks at which chip is selected | Renders, click does *nothing at all* — no handler wired, not even local state |
| **Add to Bag** (`onAddToBag`) | Real — calls `addItemToNewOrExistingBasket`, but always for the default variant, ignoring the chip | Renders, click does *nothing at all* — no handler wired |
| **Notify Me** (`onNotifyMe`) | Never rendered — `onNotifyMe` is never supplied anywhere in this codebase, and the component itself gates `showNotifyMe` on `Boolean(onNotifyMe)` being true, so it correctly never appears rather than appearing-and-lying |

**So there are two different bug classes here, not one:**
1. **PLP's size-chip selection is genuinely cosmetic** (visual only, no effect on what ships) — the one you already found.
2. **Recently-Viewed's size chips *and* Add to Bag aren't cosmetic — they're not wired at all** (confirmed last time: clicks land, nothing happens, no request, no error).

**Why Notify Me never has this problem, and PLP/Recently-Viewed's `showBag`/`showSizeChips` do:** `showNotifyMe` is *computed* — `Boolean(isUnavailable) && Boolean(onNotifyMe)` — so it structurally cannot render without a real handler behind it. `showBag`/`showSizeChips` are read straight off the static `VARIATION_CONFIG` table with no such check. That's the actual root design gap: the component has already solved this exact problem once, just for one control and not the other two.

**One more related, adjacent finding, not the same question but worth knowing:** neither mapper computes `isUnavailable` for Recently-Viewed at all (PLP's own mapper does, via `hit.orderable === false`). So a sold-out product would render on the Full History page as if fully orderable — no notify-me, no unavailable state, size chips and Add to Bag all looking normal for a product that can't actually be ordered.

**The structural fix that would close all of this at once:** apply the same co-requirement pattern already proven for `showNotifyMe` to the other two — `showBag = config.showBag && Boolean(onAddToBag)`, `showSizeChips = config.showSizeChips && Boolean(onSizeChipSelect)`. That would make Recently-Viewed's currently-inert controls disappear entirely (honest, if incomplete) instead of appearing to work, and would prevent this exact class of bug for any future consumer that forgets to wire a handler — without needing to touch either page's own business logic.

ELI5: two button wiring problems; fix is conditional rendering
text:
Two separate problems wearing the same disguise — buttons that look like they work.

**PLP's size chips:** like an elevator button that lights up when you press it, but the elevator was already going to that floor regardless of what you pressed. You get visual feedback (the chip highlights), but it doesn't actually change what you get.

**Recently Viewed's size chips and Add to Bag:** more like a button that's just glued onto the wall — not wired to anything at all. You press it, nothing lights up, nothing happens, because there's genuinely no wire behind it.

**Notify Me never has this problem, and here's the simple reason why:** the component has a built-in rule — "don't show this button at all unless something real is actually plugged in behind it." So Notify Me correctly stays hidden everywhere, rather than showing up and lying to you. Add to Bag and Size Chips never got that same rule — they show up whether or not anything's wired behind them, which is exactly how both problems above were able to happen in the first place.

**The fix:** give Add to Bag and Size Chips the same "don't show up unless you're actually wired to something" rule Notify Me already has. That alone would make Recently Viewed's dead buttons disappear instead of sitting there pretending to work — and stops the same mistake from happening again on any future page that forgets to wire a handler.

Before implementing, let me trace through the actual consequences precisely — there's a subtlety in how `hoverHidesPrice`/`hoverRevealsSizeSelector` are derived that could matter here.

Tracing this through carefully surfaces something the naive version of the fix would get wrong. Let me lay out the actual expected result, not just the intended one.

**The straightforward part — gating `showBag`/`showSizeChips` on handler presence:**

- **PLP**: zero visible change. Its wrapper (`ProductListCard`) always supplies a real `onSizeChipSelect`, and `handleAddToBag` is always passed too — so both stay `true`, both controls keep rendering exactly as today. This fix doesn't touch PLP's own "selection is cosmetic" problem at all — that's still the separate fork we discussed, untouched by this.
- **Recently-Viewed Grid**: `onAddToBag`/`onSizeChipSelect` are never supplied → both flags become `false` → **the size-chip row and the Add to Bag button disappear entirely** from every card on the Full History page.

**The part that isn't obvious, and would be a real regression if missed:** `hoverHidesPrice` and `hoverRevealsSizeSelector` are computed completely independently —

```ts
const hoverHidesPrice = config.hoverHidesPrice && !isUnavailable;
const hoverRevealsSizeSelector = config.hoverRevealsSizeSelector && !isUnavailable;
```

— with no reference to whether `onSizeChipSelect` exists at all. If I only touch `showBag`/`showSizeChips` and leave these two alone, then on Recently-Viewed: hovering a card would still try to *hide the price* "in favour of the size-chip reveal" — except the size-chip region no longer renders at all. Net result: **hovering a card makes the price disappear with nothing replacing it** — worse than today, where at least the price stays put.

So the real fix needs `hoverHidesPrice`/`hoverRevealsSizeSelector` gated the same way — on whether there's actually something to reveal, not just on `isUnavailable`.

**Expected end state, once done correctly:**
- **PLP**: nothing changes, at all.
- **Recently-Viewed**: cards show image, badge, name, price only — no size chips, no Add to Bag, and price stays visible on hover instead of vanishing. That's not a new, unproven layout — it's the exact same shape the `home` variation already ships with today (`showBag: false, showSizeChips: false` there too), so it's a known-good rendering state, not something untested.

**What this fix explicitly does *not* do:** it doesn't make Recently-Viewed's size selection or Add to Bag actually work — it makes the currently-broken controls honestly disappear instead of pretending to work. Building the real thing (per-card selection state + a real basket mutation, per the PLP-pattern-vs-build-it-correctly fork from earlier) is still a separate, later step.

detail: no handler for notify me - what does that mean? ELI5
explained 'no handler' meaning: button exists, wiring not yet built
text:
"Handler" is just the instructions for "what happens when someone presses this." No handler means the button is real and pressable, but there's nothing written down for what should happen next — so pressing it does exactly nothing. No error, no action, no reaction. It's like a doorbell that's installed and looks completely normal, but isn't actually wired to a chime yet — you can press it all day, nothing rings.

In this case, that's intentional, not a bug: we're choosing to install the doorbell now (so the button is visibly there, in the right spot) before the wiring behind it — the actual "notify me when it's back" feature — gets built later.

Let me check if there's a missing `expand` value that would unlock this before concluding it's structurally unavailable.

Confirmed. Root cause found — and it's a one-line config gap, not a structural endpoint limitation.

## What's actually happening

**`overrides/app/pages/product-list/index.tsx:257`** requests:
```ts
expand: ['promotions', 'variations', 'prices', 'images', 'page_meta_tags', 'custom_properties']
```

The Search endpoint's own SDK documentation states its `expand` parameter **defaults to `availability, images, prices, represented_products, variations`** when you don't pass one at all. But this page *does* pass an explicit list — and passing one **replaces** the default rather than adding to it. `'availability'` isn't in that list, so it's being silently switched off for every PLP search call.

That matters because `orderable` is documented, real SDK data — not something exclusive to the Product Detail endpoint as I'd assumed earlier:

> `VariationAttributeValue.orderable`: *"A flag indicating whether at least one variant with this variation attribute value is available to sell."*

That's the exact field `selectSizeChipValues` already reads (`value.orderable === false`). With `availability` excluded from `expand`, SFCC never populates it, so it's `undefined` on every value, and `undefined === false` is always `false` — every chip renders enabled regardless of real stock. Confirmed directly against `4673TS251`'s live SSR payload: every value in its `size` attribute has no `orderable` key at all.

**So the size-chip logic itself was never broken** — `isDisabled: value.orderable === false` is exactly correct. It's been reading a field the request never asked the API to fill in.

## Proposed fix

Add `'availability'` to that one `expand` array. Since it's part of SFCC's own default set, this isn't new/heavier data — it's restoring what a plain unconfigured call already gets for free.

**One adjacent thing worth flagging while I'm in this exact array**: the default list also includes `represented_products`, which this page's explicit list is *also* currently suppressing. That's relevant because `ProductListCard`'s fallback I added this session (`resolved?.productId ?? hit.representedProduct?.id ?? hit.productId`) depends on `hit.representedProduct` — which may be silently `undefined` today for the same reason. Worth confirming/fixing in the same pass since it's the same root cause, same line, same file.

Want me to go ahead and add both to the `expand` array, then verify live against `4673TS251` (size "1" should show disabled) the same way I confirmed the bug?

text:
Same component, same variation — but not identical, and I found one more real gap while comparing the two mappers side by side.

**Yes — literally the same `ZimmProductCard` at `variation: 'plp'`.** Both mappers (`productListCardMapper.ts` for PLP, `recentlyViewedFullHistoryCard.ts` for Full History) produce the exact same TypeScript output shape (`ZimmProductCardBaseProps & ZimmProductCardPlpVariation`), and `recentlyViewedFullHistoryCard.ts` was deliberately written as a near-verbatim port of PLP's mapper for this reason — same gallery-picking logic, same size-chip logic, same was/now pricing logic, all ported line-for-line.

**But real differences exist, because the two pages read from different SFCC endpoints** (PLP hits Shopper **Search**; Full History hits Shopper **Products** `getProducts`) — not by design intent, just because those endpoints return different data:

1. **Badge never shows on Full History** (already self-documented in the file itself) — `getProducts` has no confirmed badge field the way a Search hit does. Same product, badge on PLP, no badge here.

2. **🔴 `isUnavailable` is never set on Full History at all — this one wasn't flagged anywhere.** PLP's mapper sets `isUnavailable: hit.orderable === false`. I just read `recentlyViewedFullHistoryCard.ts`'s full return object line-by-line — there's no `isUnavailable` field in it, period. That flag drives real behavior on `ZimmProductCard`: the whole disabled/dimmed recipe state, and (since this session's Notify-Me change) whether the Notify Me button shows at all. A genuinely out-of-stock product would look and behave as fully available on this page, while the identical product on PLP would show correctly. Individual size chips still correctly show per-size disabled state (that part *is* wired via `sizeChipValues[].isDisabled`) — it's specifically the card-level unavailability that's missing.

3. **Add to Bag does nothing** (found last turn) — button renders, click has no handler.

4. **Size chips aren't selectable** (found last turn) — chips render with correct per-size availability, but there's no state/handler to select one.

5. **No size-aware variant resolution exists for this page at all.** PLP's mapper exports `resolveOrderableVariant` (resolves a selected size to its real SKU/price). `recentlyViewedFullHistoryCard.ts` has no equivalent — so fixing #3/#4 isn't just "wire up the same handler PLP uses," that resolution logic would need building here too. The raw data may well be there already (`recentlyViewedProductFetch.ts` does request `expand: ['variations']`), just nothing reads it yet.

Everything else — price (was/now via `getPriceData`), gallery images, size-chip disabled states, the image-fallback cascade — is genuinely identical logic between the two, verified directly, not just assumed from the port.

So: same card, same look, but three real behavioral gaps (badge, unavailability, and the two interactive pieces) between what a shopper sees on PLP versus what they'd see for the identical product on Full History.

hover-swap wiring missing in PLP; need image-type discriminator
text:
Confirmed — you're right, this is a real, missed gap. Not from the plan/spec side; the mechanism was built correctly, but the real data feeding it was never wired up on PLP.

**The mechanism is fully built and correctly enabled for PLP:**
- `VARIATION_CONFIG.plp.showHoverImageSwap: true` (confirmed a few turns back when I read the table directly).
- `ZimmProductCard` wires it correctly: `swapOnHover={config.showHoverImageSwap && Boolean(hoverImage)}`.
- `ZimmProductCardMedia` correctly crossfades `primaryImage` → `hoverImage` when `swapOnHover` is true.

**But `productListCardMapper.ts` never populates `hoverImage` at all** — I just grepped it directly, zero matches. Same for `product-list/index.tsx`'s own spread chain — zero matches there too. Since `hoverImage` is always `undefined` for every PLP card, `Boolean(hoverImage)` always evaluates `false`, so `swapOnHover` always evaluates `false` regardless of the config flag being `true`. **The swap can never fire on PLP today, no matter what.**

This isn't a spec ambiguity, either — it's from SFCC-236's own confirmed PLP hover behaviour (the plan I read earlier cites Jasmijn's comment: hover reveals size-selector, hides price, swaps to a model photo — already-shipped PLP behaviour, not something new). The mapper just never got that piece wired when it was built (its own docblock even calls itself a "quick test integration," which lines up with primary image + gallery being covered but this one being missed).

One thing I haven't verified yet, and would need to before fixing it: what image data actually distinguishes a "model" shot from the primary/flat-lay shot in this catalog's `imageGroups` — I don't have that confirmed in this session. Want me to go check that next, or hold here?

That makes 6 identified PLP gaps total — 4 fixed, and now 2 open (the image-fallback cascade from before, and this hover-swap wiring).

detail: tell me something: when a product is out of stock, what happens on hover? what shows? product name + what?
out-of-stock hover: name + price + disabled bag + 'Notify me' CTA
text:
Traced through the actual recipe CSS (`zimmProductCard.css.ts`) and the organism's own flag derivation — this one's fully built and Figma-confirmed already, not a gap. Here's exactly what shows, for an out-of-stock PLP card on Desktop:

**Default state (before you hover):**
- Product name
- Price — stays visible (out-of-stock gets an "additive" treatment on Desktop, not a swap)
- Bag icon — visible, but disabled/greyed out, cursor `not-allowed`
- Size chips — **never shown**, in any state, on any device, once a product is unavailable (`sizeSelectorUnavailable`'s own unconditional hide — there's nothing to pick a size *for* when nothing's in stock)

**On hover, the one thing that changes:**
- **"Notify me" appears** — it's hidden by default and only reveals once you actually hover (or keyboard-focus) the card. Everything else above stays exactly as it was — price doesn't hide, the bag icon doesn't change.

So to answer directly: **product name + price + a disabled bag icon are already showing before you even hover — hovering only adds "Notify me."** No size-selector swap happens at all for an out-of-stock item (that's reserved for an available product, which swaps price → size chips on hover instead).

This is all deliberate and already fixed correctly — it went through several named fix rounds (Fix C, F, G, J, K) each tied to a specific Figma reference (Desktop/Hover/Unavailable node `40002163:41468`), including catching and fixing a real accessibility regression along the way (`display: none` removing these from the tab order, since replaced with a `position`/`clipPath` technique that keeps them keyboard-reachable). Unlike the hover-image-swap gap from a couple turns ago, this one isn't something we need to add — it's solid.

detail: how is the PLP product card configured now? does it implement this behavior: "product name + price + a disabled bag icon are already showing before you even hover — hovering only adds "Notify me."" ?
PLP unavailable card: name+price+disabled bag shown; hover adds Notify Me
text:
Yes — confirmed again, from the actual prop derivation this time, not just the CSS rules alone. Here's the exact chain, for `variation: 'plp'` + `isUnavailable: true`:

**Step 1 — `index.tsx`'s own derivation (lines 535–563), computed once per card:**
```
hoverHidesPrice          = config.hoverHidesPrice && !isUnavailable        → true && !true  = false
hoverRevealsSizeSelector = config.hoverRevealsSizeSelector && !isUnavailable → true && !true = false
sizeSelectorUnavailable  = config.hoverRevealsSizeSelector && isUnavailable  → true && true  = true
hoverRevealsNotifyMe     = showNotifyMe (= Boolean(isUnavailable))          → true
bagHiddenOnMobile        = config.hideBagOnMobile || (...)                  → true (mobile-width only, doesn't touch Desktop)
```

**Step 2 — what those four values actually do in `zimmProductCard.css.ts`, on Desktop:**

| Element | Rule that fires | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Price | `sizeSelectorUnavailable` hides it unconditionally, but the paired `[DESKTOP_QUERY]` block explicitly sets it back to `display: 'block'` | **Visible, unaffected by hover** — `hoverHidesPrice` is `false`, so no hover-hide rule even exists for this card |
| Size chips | `sizeSelectorUnavailable` hides it unconditionally — no `[DESKTOP_QUERY]` override exists for this one | **Never shown, in any state** |
| Bag icon | `hideBagOnMobile` only applies below `DESKTOP_QUERY`; at Desktop width it's shown again as `display: 'flex'`. Separately, `ZimmProductCardContent` sets `disabled={isUnavailable}` | **Visible, disabled/greyed out, always — hover doesn't change it** |
| Notify Me | `hoverRevealsNotifyMe: true` → hidden by default (`clipPath: inset(50%)`) inside `HOVER_CAPABLE_QUERY`, revealed only on `&:hover`/`&:has(:focus-visible)` | **Hidden until hover, then appears** |

So yes — exactly as stated: **name + price + a disabled bag icon are already on screen before you even touch the card; hovering adds only "Notify me."** Nothing else moves. That's what's actually configured right now, not just what should be — traced from the real derivation logic, not assumed from the CSS alone.

detail: so the only thing missing from PLP product card is the functionality of swap the image on hover?
two image gaps in PLP mapper: hoverImage + primaryImageFallbacks
text:
Not quite — there are two, not one. Both are image-related and both come from the same root cause (PLP's mapper doesn't supply certain image fields), but they're functionally different gaps:

1. **Hover-to-model-image swap** (the one you just named) — `hoverImage` is never populated by `productListCardMapper.ts`, so `swapOnHover` always evaluates `false` regardless of the `showHoverImageSwap: true` config.

2. **Broken-image fallback cascade** (found a few turns earlier, before the hover-swap one) — `primaryImageFallbacks` was built and wired into the Rail's and Full History's own mappers, but never into PLP's. Same underlying defect we found live on `4673TS251` (a 404'd image sitting ahead of working ones) is still unprotected on PLP specifically.

Both trace back to the exact same file never being updated — `productListCardMapper.ts` — just for two different props (`hoverImage` vs `primaryImageFallbacks`). Everything else we checked for PLP (size-chip disabled state, size-aware Add to Bag, Notify Me, was/now pricing, badge, `isUnavailable`, the whole hover-reveal state machine) is confirmed correctly wired and shipped.

So: two open items on PLP's product card, both in the same mapper file, not just the hover swap alone.

demo approach: hoverImage = imageGroups.medium[1]; PLP avoids broken image by accident (reads hit.image, not imageGroups)
text:
That fully explains it — real data, not luck. Let me also pull the demo branch's approach for the hover-swap, without touching the current working tree.

Both confirmed, with hard evidence. Here's each.

## 1. Hover-image-swap — the demo branch's approach

`overrides/app/pages/home/liveProductCardDemoMapper.ts` on `feature/zimmproductcard-live-demo` (read directly via `git show`, without switching branches):

```ts
const groups = filterImageGroups(hit.imageGroups ?? [], {
  viewType: 'medium',
  variationValues: variant.colourCode ? { color: variant.colourCode } : {},
});
const groupImages = groups?.[0]?.images ?? [];

primaryImage: groupImages[0] ? toCardImage(groupImages[0]) : ...,
hoverImage: groupImages[1] ? toCardImage(groupImages[1]) : undefined,
images: groupImages.length > 1 ? groupImages.map(toCardImage) : undefined,
```

**The approach is purely positional, not semantic.** `hoverImage` isn't resolved via any special "model shot" viewType or tag — it's just **the second image (index 1) in the same medium-viewType image group** that also supplies `primaryImage` (index 0) and the full gallery. One filtered array feeds all three.

One real difference from PLP's current mapper, worth flagging before porting this: the demo scopes that filter to the **resolved variant's own colour** (`variationValues: {color: ...}`) — PLP's own `selectGalleryImages` today picks "whichever image group has the most images," with no viewType or colour filter at all. So porting this exact approach isn't just "add one field" — it'd also mean aligning PLP's image-group selection to be colour/viewType-aware the way the demo's is.

## 2. Why PLP renders 4673TS251 fine but the Rail doesn't

Pulled the live SSR JSON properly (parsed `#mobify-data`'s actual JSON, not a text-window grep — my first attempt at this literally bled into a neighboring product's data and gave a wrong answer, caught and redone correctly) and compared the two fields side by side:

| Source | Field read | Filename |
|---|---|---|
| **PLP** (`hit.image`, flat Search-hit field) | image index **9** | `9.4673ts251.gvscp.guava-seascape.jpg` |
| **Rail/Full-History** (`imageGroups.medium[0]`) | image index **1** | `1.4673ts251.gvscp.guava-seascape.jpg` |

**They're different images, from two different fields entirely** — and index 1 of the medium group is the specific one already confirmed broken. PLP isn't handling the broken image better; it simply never looks at it, because its mapper reads SFCC's own single pre-picked `hit.image` field instead of walking `imageGroups` directly.

That means the PLP fallback gap I flagged is still real, not disproven by this — it's coincidence that `hit.image` happens to point somewhere safe for this specific product. If `hit.image` itself were ever the broken asset for some other product, PLP has zero protection today, same as Rail did before the fix.

detail: ELI5BITFLOTP
ELI5BITFLOTP decoded: hover-swap uses pic #2, PLP/Recently Viewed differ on photo source
text:
**1. Hover-swap in the demo — simpler than it sounds.** It doesn't hunt for a special "model photo." It just takes whatever the **second picture** is in that product's normal photo set — picture #1 stays as the default image, picture #2 is what shows on hover. No tagging, no special logic, just "next photo in line." One catch: the demo also narrows those photos down to just the ones matching the exact colour the shopper picked — PLP doesn't do that narrowing today at all, so copying this isn't a one-line fix, it also means teaching PLP to care about colour when picking photos.

**2. Why PLP shows the picture fine but Recently Viewed doesn't, same product.** They're not looking at the same photo at all. PLP grabs the one "official" picture SFCC itself hands back for search results — for this product, that happens to be photo #9, and #9 works fine. Recently Viewed instead reaches straight into the full photo album and grabs photo #1 — and #1, for this exact product, is the broken one. So PLP isn't doing anything smarter — it's just looking somewhere else entirely, by coincidence. Which means PLP still has zero backup plan if its own "official" picture is ever the broken one on some other product — this one just got lucky.

detail: question for item #1, how would colour be considered if there's no color selector in the product card, especially for products that have multiple colors - does sfcc ship a variant of a product that's set/marked/tagged as the default?
Checking for master-product / default-variant markers in the SDK's Product type
confirmed SFCC marks default variant via representedProduct.c_color
text:
Real, important gap in the demo's own approach — worth flagging directly: **the demo branch didn't actually solve this.** Its own hand-rolled type (`LiveDemoSourceHit`) has no `representedProduct` field at all, and its `resolveDemoVariant` just picks "first orderable variant, or variants[0]" — an arbitrary pick, not anything SFCC marked as default. So copying that approach as-is wouldn't answer your question; it would just grab *some* variant, not necessarily the one SFCC treats as representative.

**Is there a real SFCC "default variant" signal? Sort of — but only for a Search hit, and not a guaranteed typed contract.**

I checked the actual SDK type for `representedProduct` (what a `ProductSearchHit` carries): it's typed as `{id: string} & {[key: string]: any}` — just an ID, plus an open-ended catch-all. But in the **live data** I pulled from PLP last turn, that object actually carried real extra fields:
```
"representedProduct": { "id": "4673TS251GVSCP0P", "c_color": "GVSCP", ... }
```
So for this catalog, `representedProduct` does look like SFCC's own pick of "the one variant that represents this hit" — colour included, via `c_color`. That's exactly the kind of default-variant marker you're asking about. Two honest caveats:

1. **This lives on the Search endpoint only.** `getProducts` (what Rail/Full-History's own fetch uses) returns a master `Product` with a `master` field (`masterId`, `orderable`, `price`/`priceMax`) — no equivalent "here's the representative variant" pointer at all. So even if PLP used this, it wouldn't transfer to Rail/Full-History — different endpoint, no such signal exists there.
2. **I've only confirmed `c_color` is populated for this one product's live data**, not that it's reliably there for every hit across the catalog — since it falls through an untyped index signature, it's whatever this catalog's search-index config happens to expose, not an SDK guarantee.

**One more thing worth noticing:** PLP's `hit.image` (the flat field it already uses today) is almost certainly already built by SFCC from that same representative variant — so PLP is already implicitly showing "the default colour's photo" without any code on our side choosing it. The real missing piece for a hover image isn't "figure out the default colour" — SFCC's already doing that for the primary shot — it's getting a **second** photo for that same already-resolved variant, which would mean scoping `filterImageGroups` by `representedProduct.c_color` (if it holds up across more products) rather than inventing a separate "first orderable" pick the way the demo did.

detail: question for item #1: for products with multiple colors/variants how is it decided which one gets shown in the product card - this is related to you mentioning narrowing down which colour the shopper picked because in our product cards, no color select is available as opposed to the ootb product card which as the color selector
Searching live PLP data for a genuine multi-colour product and inspecting its structure
Inspecting the full structure of each medium image group for the multi-colour product
found primary img defers to SFCC color pick; gallery logic ignores it
text:
Checked with real live data — found a genuine two-colour product on the current PLP results (`ZWNEWPRD04`, BLK/TAN) and traced through exactly what happens.

**Short answer: it's decided entirely server-side, before our code ever sees the data — and there's no client-side colour logic in this card at all, which matches what you noticed.**

For `ZWNEWPRD04`:
- `representedProduct.id` = `ZWNEWPRD04BLK0`, `representedProduct.c_color` = **`BLK`** — SFCC's search index has already picked Black as "the" representative colour for this one search hit, before it ever reaches the frontend.
- `hit.image` (the flat field PLP's mapper reads for the primary image) is filename `ZWNEWPRD04.BLK.PZ.jpg` — consistent with that same BLK pre-selection. So the primary photo you see is always whatever colour SFCC itself decided was representative — we have zero input into that choice, same as you observed there's no selector to give a shopper that input either.

**But here's a real, new gap this surfaced.** I dug into `imageGroups` for this product and each colour has its own separate, explicitly-tagged group:

```
medium group 1: variationAttributes: [{id: "color", values: [{value: "BLK"}]}] → BLK photos
medium group 2: variationAttributes: [{id: "color", values: [{value: "TAN"}]}] → TAN photos
```

PLP's own `selectGalleryImages` (the function that builds the swipeable multi-image gallery) does **not** filter by colour, or even by viewType — it just picks "whichever image group across the entire array has the most images." With BLK and TAN groups both sitting in that same array, it's picking essentially at random which colour's photos populate the gallery — it could easily show TAN images in the gallery on a card whose primary photo (and represented colour) is BLK. That's inconsistent with SFCC's own colour pre-selection, and it's a different, arguably bigger problem than the missing hover-image swap — a real mismatch a shopper could actually see, not just a missing feature.

So to tie this back to your original question: since there's no colour selector on our card, the honest picture is "we fully defer to SFCC's pick for the *primary* image, but the *gallery* logic ignores that pick entirely and can disagree with it."

detail: given the findings that the representing colour/variant for a product is decided server-side - how should selectGalleryImages work/handle it then?
Checking whether hit.variants carries a colour key and whether representedProduct.id resolves to a real variant
selectGalleryImages fix mapped (colour + viewType); awaiting go-ahead
text:
Given that, here's what I'd recommend — and I verified the mechanism against the same live product before proposing it, not just theorizing.

**The core fix: resolve the representative colour from data already on the hit, then scope the gallery to it.**

I checked `ZWNEWPRD04` again, specifically whether `hit.variants` can be matched against `hit.representedProduct.id` to get the colour SFCC already picked:

```
representedProduct.id: ZWNEWPRD04BLK0
variants: ZWNEWPRD04BLK0 -> {color: 'BLK', size: '0'}   ← exact match
```

It resolves cleanly and deterministically — no guessing, no reliance on the `c_color` custom attribute (which is untyped and catalog-specific), no string-parsing an ID. This is actually more reliable than what the demo branch does (its `resolveDemoVariant` picks "first orderable variant" as a heuristic, because it has no `representedProduct` to anchor against) — PLP's hit already tells us exactly which variant is representative.

**So the fix, concretely:**
1. Find the matching variant: `hit.variants?.find(v => v.productId === hit.representedProduct?.id)`.
2. Read its `variationValues?.color`.
3. Pass that into `filterImageGroups(hit.imageGroups, {viewType: 'medium', variationValues: {color: representativeColour}})` — the same base-SFCC utility, same shape, the demo branch already proved works.
4. Build the gallery from *that* filtered group only, not "whichever group anywhere has the most images."

**One thing worth calling out — this fixes two bugs at once, not one.** Today's `selectGalleryImages` has no `viewType` filter either, so it isn't just risking the wrong colour — it could just as easily pull from a `large` or `small` group instead of `medium`, if that group happens to have more images. Adding the `viewType: 'medium'` filter (which `selectPrimaryImage` on the Rail/Full-History side already does correctly) needs to happen regardless of the colour fix.

**Fallback for when this can't resolve** (single-colour product, or a hit with no `variants`/`representedProduct` data): degrade to today's "biggest group" heuristic, but at least scoped to `viewType: 'medium'` first — never fully unfiltered.

**One open question I can't answer from this data alone:** `hit.image` (the primary photo) already happened to agree with the representative colour for both products I checked — but I don't have confirmation that's a guaranteed SFCC behavior versus a coincidence of this test catalog. Worth keeping in mind, though I have no counter-evidence to suggest fixing the primary image too.

Want me to turn this into a plan step, or hold here?

detail: once we get this done and resolved, what would this mean for the on hover image swap?
gallery vs hover-swap mutually exclusive; need product policy
text:
Good question — and the honest answer is: it doesn't come for free, because there's a real conflict in the component itself that the demo's approach papers over.

**The part that IS free:** the same colour+viewType-scoped array (`groupImages`) that fixes the gallery is exactly the raw material hover-swap needs too — no separate resolution work, same lookup.

**The part that isn't free — a real conflict I need to flag before this becomes an implementation.** I went back and re-checked `ZimmProductCardMedia`'s actual logic:

```ts
const gallery = images && images.length > 1 ? images : undefined;
const showHoverSwap = swapOnHover && Boolean(hoverImage) && !gallery;
```

**Gallery mode and hover-swap are mutually exclusive by design** — the instant `images.length > 1`, `gallery` is truthy, and `!gallery` forces `showHoverSwap` to `false` regardless of whether `hoverImage` is populated.

Now look at what the demo mapper actually does: `hoverImage = groupImages[1]`, `images = groupImages.length > 1 ? groupImages : undefined`. Both conditions trigger off the exact same thing — "is there a 2nd image." **Which means: any time `hoverImage` gets populated, `images` gets populated too, with the same length, and gallery mode wins every time.** Hover-swap can never actually fire from that construction — it's live data, but functionally dead code, for any product with 2+ images (which was most of them — 4673TS251 alone had 9).

This actually lines up with something in the original AC I read earlier: Jasmijn's comment separately calls out "swaps to a model photo" and "shows carousel arrows for multi-image" as two distinct things — not one behavior. That reads like the real intent was never "always do both," it's "pick one, per product": a genuine multi-angle gallery gets the carousel treatment; a product with just a flat-lay + one model shot gets the hover-swap instead.

**So the actual decision needed once the gallery fix lands:** given the correctly-scoped `groupImages` for a product, we need a rule for which mode it gets — my instinct, matching the AC's own split, would be something like: exactly 2 images → hover-swap (primary + model shot, no gallery); 3+ images → gallery/carousel, skip `hoverImage` entirely so it doesn't quietly go dead. That's a real product decision though, not mine to default silently — want me to check how many images a few real multi-colour products actually have in their scoped group, to see how often each case would even come up before you decide?

Real numbers, across every product on the page (7 total, colour + viewType-scoped medium count each):

| Product | Colour | Images (scoped) |
|---|---|---|
| 4673TS251 | GVSCP | 9 |
| 8637DS241 | BLUBIR | 6 |
| ZWNEWPRD04 | BLK | 2 |
| ZWNEWPRD03 | PNK | 2 |
| ZWNEWPRD01 | RED | 2 |

| 25519318M | JJI15XX | 2 |

**5 of 7 (71%) sit at exactly 2 images; the other 2 have a fuller 6–9-image set.** Exactly-2 isn't an edge case here — it's the common case in this catalog.

Given that, and given you want hover-swap **and** gallery active together rather than one-or-the-other, here's the real implication: **this can't be done in the mapper alone.** `ZimmProductCardMedia`'s own gating today is:

```ts
const showHoverSwap = swapOnHover && Boolean(hoverImage) && !gallery;
```

That `!gallery` is an unconditional block — as long as it's there, gallery mode always wins and hover-swap can never fire alongside it, regardless of what the mapper supplies. Making both happen together means that line itself has to change (drop or restructure the `!gallery` condition), not just fixing `selectGalleryImages` and populating `hoverImage` upstream.

Practically, once that's changed, here's what it'd look like given the real numbers above: for the common 2-image case, hovering crossfades to image #2 *and* reveals carousel arrows to page between the two. For the fuller 6–9-image products, hovering crossfades to image #2 as an immediate preview while the arrows let the shopper carousel through the rest — a genuinely richer interaction, not just redundant with itself.

So the real scope, once you're ready to build this: a mapper-level fix (colour/viewType-scoped `selectGalleryImages` + populate `hoverImage`) **plus** a component-level change to `ZimmProductCardMedia`'s hover gating. Want me to fold both into a plan?

detail: what's our finding? ELI5
multi-colour photo bug root cause: card ignores SFCC colour; fix: filter by colour + allow hover+gallery together
text:
**The finding, plain and simple:**

1. **Multi-colour products can show the wrong colour's photos.** The card doesn't check which colour it's actually looking at when picking photos — it just grabs whatever photo batch happens to have the most images. Since each colour has its own separate batch, this can accidentally mix in the wrong one.

2. **The store already picked the right colour — the card just wasn't listening.** SFCC decides which colour represents each product tile before our code ever sees it. We proved the data's there and reliable (colour code lines up perfectly every time we checked) — so the fix isn't "build a colour picker," it's "actually read the colour SFCC already chose, and only show that colour's photos."

3. **Marcel already built a working example of this** on the demo branch — filter down to one colour before picking anything.

4. **Checked real products: most have just 2 photos once correctly filtered** (5 of 7 checked); a couple of the fuller ones have 6–9.

5. **Hover needs to do two things at once, and the code currently only allows one.** On hover, the card should both swap the photo AND turn on the gallery arrows — but there's a rule today that says "if a real photo gallery exists, skip the hover-swap." That rule has to change too, not just the photo-picking.

So: two real fixes needed — how photos get picked (respect the colour SFCC already chose), and a rule in the card component itself that currently blocks hover-swap and gallery mode from running together.

Checking SDK doc comment for ProductSearchHit's image field
Comparing hit.image against every viewType's own first image for two real products
confirmed SFCC search returns per-product viewtype images; PLP/Recently Viewed strategy validated
text:
Confirmed directly from the SDK's own doc comment on `ProductSearchHit.image`:

> **"The first image of the product hit for the configured viewtype."**

So "official" means: **whichever image viewtype SFCC's Search configuration is set to use for search results, first image in that group** — a Business Manager setting, not anything visible or controllable from our frontend code.

**And it's not even a fixed viewtype across every product — I checked two real ones and got two different answers:**
- **4673TS251**: `hit.image` (photo "9") exactly matches this product's `hi-res` viewtype's own first image.
- **ZWNEWPRD04**: `hit.image` matches its `large` viewtype's first image — because this product has **no `hi-res` group at all**, so search evidently falls back to the next available viewtype.

So "official" isn't one consistent thing we could replicate — it's SFCC's own resolved answer, per-product, based on whatever viewtypes exist for that specific item. That's exactly why trying to guess/reconstruct it ourselves would be fragile — better to just keep trusting it as the primary source, like your proposal.

**Your proposed approach is the right one, and it ties together everything else we found today.** Keep `hit.image` as-is for the primary photo (fully respecting whatever SFCC decided is official — no change needed there), and populate `primaryImageFallbacks` from the **same colour + `medium`-viewtype-scoped group** we already need to correctly resolve for the gallery/hover-swap fix. If the official pick ever 404s, it falls back to a real, correctly-scoped photo from that product's own medium gallery — the exact mechanism already proven on Rail/Full-History.

That means one piece of resolution logic (colour-scoped, `medium`-viewtype images) now feeds **three** things: the gallery fix, the hover-swap image, and PLP's fallback safety net — not three separate problems.

| 4 | Was/now pricing was hardcoded off | Wired real `getPriceData` into the mapper |

## Open, now with a concrete plan — three gaps, one shared fix

**The root problem behind all three:** `productListCardMapper.ts` never resolves *which colour* it's looking at for a multi-colour product. That single gap is what's causing all of the below.

**The fix:** resolve the representative colour deterministically — match `hit.representedProduct.id` against `hit.variants[]`, read that variant's `variationValues.color` (verified working on real live data, no guessing). Feed that colour into `filterImageGroups(imageGroups, {viewType: 'medium', variationValues: {color}})` — the same call the `feature/zimmproductcard-live-demo` branch already proved out. **That one resolved array now feeds three separate fixes:**

| # | Finding | How this fix closes it |
|---|---|---|
| 5 | Gallery images (`selectGalleryImages`) aren't scoped by colour *or* viewtype — can show a mix of the wrong colour's photos, or pull from `large`/`small` instead of `medium` | Rebuild it from the colour+viewtype-scoped array instead of "whichever group has the most images" |
| 6 | No hover-to-model-photo swap on PLP (`hoverImage` never populated) | Populate `hoverImage` from the same scoped array |
| 7 | No fallback if the primary photo 404s (PLP never got this, unlike Rail/Full History) | Keep `hit.image` ("the official picture," confirmed to be a backend-configured viewtype pick — not something we should try to replicate) as primary, but supply `primaryImageFallbacks` from that same scoped array as backup candidates |

**One more piece, and it's a real code change, not just data-wiring:** you've confirmed the hover behaviour should show the model-photo swap **and** activate the gallery arrows together — but `ZimmProductCardMedia` today has a rule (`&& !gallery`) that only ever allows one or the other. That rule itself needs to change for #6 to actually be visible whenever a real gallery exists (which real data shows is common — 5 of 7 sampled products had exactly 2 images once correctly scoped, 2 had 6–9).

**Bottom line:** 4 fixed, 3 open — and the 3 open ones aren't 3 separate investigations anymore, they're one shared data-resolution fix plus one small component-level rule change.

text:
Here's the whole thing, start to finish, plain language.

**The core problem, in one sentence:** PLP's product cards pick photos somewhat blindly — no awareness of which colour is being shown, no backup plan if a photo breaks, and no model-photo swap on hover even though the design calls for one — and fixing that properly means fixing the exact same weak spots on the Recently Viewed rail and Full History page too, since all three show photos the same broken way underneath.

**Step 1 — Build one shared "pick the right photos" tool.**
PLP and the other two surfaces don't get their colour information the same way: PLP's data already has the store's own pick for "which colour is this," but the Rail and Full History don't have that available to them at all — they have to guess (pick the first real option available). So we build one small toolkit with two ways to figure out the colour (one for each situation) plus one shared piece that, once it *has* a colour, goes and grabs the right photos for it. All three surfaces will use that same "grab the photos" piece — no more three different ad-hoc versions.

**Step 2 — Hook PLP's own card up to that toolkit.**
This is where PLP itself actually gets fixed: no more wrong-colour photos in the gallery, a real photo to swap to on hover, and a backup photo ready to go if the main one turns out broken.

**Step 3 — Hook the Rail and Full History up to the same toolkit.**
We pulled their old backup-photo code out a couple turns ago because it had this exact same colour-blindness bug. This step gives it back, done correctly this time, using the same shared tool PLP uses (just with the "guess the colour" version instead of "read the store's pick").

**Step 4 — Fix the one rule that's blocking hover-swap and the photo gallery from working together.**
Right now, the card component has a rule that says "if there's a real multi-photo gallery, don't also do the hover swap." You've confirmed both should happen at once, so that rule gets removed/changed here — this is the one piece that touches the shared photo *component* itself, not just the data feeding it.

**Still open, from last turn:** whether step 3 also gives Full History a hover-swap photo (its cards behave like PLP's, so it could use one) or stays strictly about the backup-photo fix for now.

**Full History's cards don't come from PLP's mapper at all.** `recentlyViewedFullHistoryCard.ts` is a completely separate, standalone file — different data source entirely (Shopper Products' `getProducts`, not Shopper Search), no shared code with `productListCardMapper.ts`, never imports from it. Fixing PLP's mapper touches zero lines of that file. Nothing "just follows."

**The one thing that's genuinely shared is the UI component** (`ZimmProductCardMedia`/`ZimmProductCard`) — Full History's cards render through the exact same component PLP's do. But even that doesn't help here: Full History's own mapper never populates `hoverImage` at all, so Step 4's fix (letting hover-swap and gallery run together) has nothing to activate for Full History regardless — it'd sit there just as inert as before. So practically speaking, **nothing meaningfully carries over to Full History once PLP is fixed.** It would keep today's colour-blind gallery bug and have zero fallback protection, sitting exactly as broken as it is right now, indefinitely, until someone deliberately goes back and rewires it.

Given that's the real tradeoff, here's the properly PLP-scoped plan:

**Step 1 — Fix PLP's own mapper directly** (`productListCardMapper.ts` + test)
Resolve colour via `representedProduct.id` matched against `variants[]`, use it to fix `selectGalleryImages`, populate `hoverImage`, populate `primaryImageFallbacks` — all built *inline*, not as a separate shared utility file. Building a "reusable across consumers" abstraction with only one real consumer is exactly the premature-generalization trap this project's own rules warn against — there's a direct precedent for this in the plan we've been working from (Open Question 9 on the Full History grid: decided *not* to build shared/reusable before a second real consumer exists).

**Step 2 — Component fix: let hover-swap and gallery run together** (`ZimmProductCardMedia` + test)
Same as before — this is genuinely about PLP's own cards working correctly, independent of anything Rail/Full History related.

That's it — two steps, both entirely PLP.

**Named and accepted, not silently dropped:** Rail and Full History keep zero fallback protection and their own unfixed colour-blind image bug after this ships. If that's meant to be temporary, it's real follow-up work for later, not something today's plan resolves as a side effect.

text:
**The problem, one more time, plain:** PLP's cards pick photos almost blindly — no awareness of which colour they're showing, no backup if a photo link is dead, and no "hover to see it on a model" swap even though the design wants one. And there's a second, separate snag: even where a swap *could* happen, a rule in the code blocks it whenever there's also a multi-photo gallery.

**Step 1 — Teach the PLP card-building code how to pick photos properly.**
All of this lives in one file: `productListCardMapper.ts` — the file that turns raw product data into what the card actually shows.

- **a) Figure out the right colour, two tries in order.** First: the store already tells us which colour it picked as "the" one for this product (a field called `representedProduct`) — use that. If that doesn't resolve for some reason, fall back to a sensible guess: the first colour option that's actually in stock, or just the first one listed if none are. Same trick your own demo branch already uses.
- **b) Use that colour to fix the photo gallery.** Right now the code just grabs "whichever batch of photos has the most images," with zero regard for colour or even photo size — so a multi-colour product can show the wrong colour's photos entirely. Fix: only look at photos matching both the right colour *and* the right photo size.
- **c) Give the card a photo to swap to on hover.** The swap feature already exists in the card's own code — it's just never been handed a second photo. Once (b) gives us the correctly-filtered list, photo #2 becomes the hover photo.
- **d) Give the card backup photos for when the main one is broken.** Same filtered list, the rest of it becomes "if the main photo 404s, try these instead" — this is the direct fix for the real broken-image bug we found live on `4673TS251`.

All four pieces stay in this one file, not split into a separate reusable toolkit — building "shared" logic before there's a second real user of it is exactly the kind of over-building this project's own rules tell us to avoid.

**Step 2 — Fix the rule blocking hover-swap and the gallery from running together.**
Different file: `ZimmProductCardMedia`, the component that actually renders the photos. Today it has a rule that says "if there's a real multi-photo gallery, skip the hover-swap." You've confirmed that's wrong — both should happen at once — so this step removes that rule.

**What you'll actually see once both land:**
- Multi-colour products show the *right* colour's photos, every time.
- Hovering swaps to a second photo.
- If there's a real gallery, the swipe arrows show up *at the same time* as that swap, not instead of it.
- A broken first photo quietly falls back to the next one instead of showing broken-image icon.

**What's deliberately left alone:** Full History and the Recently Viewed rail. Neither file gets touched by this work, so both keep today's issues (no backup photo, same colour-blind gallery bug) until that's picked up separately later — but the "guess the colour" logic from step 1a will already exist, tested and proven, when that day comes.

text: Sharp questions, and I don't think I can answer them precisely from memory — this depends on exactly how the current paging mechanism works under the hood. Let me go read the real implementation before answering. Good questions — and I read the actual implementation rather than guess, because the answer isn't obvious and reveals a real gap in "just remove `!gallery`." **The key mechanical fact:** the hover-swap crossfade is only ever rendered for **slide position 0** — it's hardcoded (`isPrimaryPosition && showHoverSwap && hoverImage`, where `isPrimaryPosition = index === 0`). Gallery paging, meanwhile, is a **real scroll container** with its own `currentIndex` state, completely independent of that crossfade — clicking an arrow calls `scrollTo()` and updates `currentIndex`, nothing about the hover crossfade touches either of those. And critically: per the mapper design we already agreed on, **`hoverImage` is the same underlying photo as `images[1]`** — image #2 in the gallery *is* the hover-swap photo, not a separate one. **(a) Hover swaps to image 2, then user clicks "next" — where do they land?** Image 2 — literally the same photo, again. The crossfade never moved the scroll position; it's still sitting at slide 0. Clicking "next" scrolls from slide 0 to slide 1, and slide 1 *is* the hover image. So yes — confirmed, this is exactly what you suspected in your last question. **(b) User pages to a different slide (not slide 0), then hovers — what happens?** Nothing visible. The crossfade markup only exists at slide 0's DOM position. If the user has scrolled to slide 2 or 3, that position is off-screen — hovering does nothing, because the slide currently in view was never given any hover behavior at all (it's rendered as a plain ``, no crossfade pair). **(c) A 2-image product — hover, then navigate:** Same as (a): images = [img1, img2], hover crossfades slide 0 to img2, "next" scrolls to slide 1 which *is* img2. Click "next" again (wraps around) → back to slide 0 → shows img1 again (not hovering anymore, so no crossfade). So a shopper effectively encounters image 2 twice, via two different mechanisms, for no added benefit. **So the honest answer to your underlying premise:** removing `!gallery` alone doesn't give you a coherent "both at once" experience — it gives you a hover-swap that's invisible except at slide 0, and that duplicates whatever the gallery's own slide 1 already shows. That's not a small tweak, it's a real design gap. **This needs a decision before I touch code:** - **Option A** — accept it: hover-swap is a "before you've paged" affordance only, and once a shopper manually navigates, it's fine that slide 1 happens to repeat what hover already showed them. - **Option B** — make `hoverImage` a genuinely distinct photo that never also appears as a gallery slide, so there's no duplicate encounter. - **Option C** — something else (e.g., re-deriving a hover treatment per whichever slide is currently in view, which would need real design/data work beyond what's planned). Which direction do you want?

**The part I got wrong in my last message:** I told you fallback protection was "back." It isn't, for this exact case, and I should have caught it before saying that. Here's why: once gallery mode is active, the component renders slide 0 directly from `images[0]` — completely bypassing the `effectivePrimaryImage`/fallback-cascade logic, which is a structurally separate code path only used when there's *no* gallery. So the `primaryImageFallbacks` mechanism we rebuilt provides **zero protection exactly where it's most likely needed** — a multi-image product with one bad photo.

1. **Extend fallback protection into gallery mode** — make slide 0 cascade through fallbacks even when a gallery is active. Likely produces the same kind of accepted duplicate we already have with Option A (a recovered slide 0 might repeat whatever slide 1 already shows).

Let me re-check this fresh rather than assume my earlier test was representative — there could be a real gap (timing, caching, or something I missed).

Found it — you're completely right, and I need to correct what I told you. My earlier check used an artificial 1-second wait *before* looking, which happened to land right at the edge of recovery — that made it look instantly fixed when it isn't.

**What's actually happening, checked with real timing:**

| When | State |
|---|---|
| Immediately on load | Broken image visible (`complete: false, naturalWidth: 0`) |
| +500ms | **Still broken** |
| +1500ms | Recovered (image #2, working) |
| +3000ms | Still recovered |

**The real reason:** the browser can't know an image is broken until it actually tries to load it and gets a response — for a remote CDN 404, that round trip genuinely takes something in the 500ms–1500ms range. Only *after* that failure fires does React's `onError` handler run and swap to the fallback candidate. There's no way to skip this — the browser has to actually ask and get told "no" before anything can react to it.

**So the honest picture:** the fallback isn't broken, but it isn't invisible either — a shopper loading this exact product's card will see a real broken-image icon for roughly a second before it self-heals. That's a genuine, visible defect, not the clean fix I described. I was wrong to call it "verified working" without checking the actual timing, not just the eventual end state.

**Two ways to actually improve this, if you want to go further:**
1. **Mask the gap** — render a neutral placeholder/skeleton in place of the image until either it loads successfully or the fallback resolves, so the shopper never sees the broken icon itself, just a brief loading state instead. Real added scope (a new visual state, not just data plumbing).
2. **Leave it as-is** — given this only affects a product whose real fix is a Business Manager re-publish, and the visible window is roughly a second, this may not be worth more engineering effort versus just getting the catalog data fixed.

it reads `large`; PLP/Rail read `medium` (per AGENTS.md's own image-sizing rule) and hit the broken one directly. This needs someone with Business Manager access to re-publish the `medium` asset for this image.
